data.title: Self-Deletion After Execution
data.summary: After establishing persistence or completing its task, the sample deletes its own executable from disk, leaving no file for later static analysis or signature scanning to find.
data.description:
Self-deletion is usually implemented as a delayed delete-on-close, a batch script spawned
to remove the parent after it exits, or a direct call that deletes the file while it is
still mapped and running (possible on Windows via a rename-then-delete trick, since an open
handle does not block deletion of the directory entry). What survives is whatever
persistence mechanism re-launches the payload from memory, a dropped copy elsewhere, or a
fileless technique — the deleted file itself is gone.
data.recommendation:
* Capture the binary before the deletion trigger fires — on first execution, from network transfer, or from memory before deletion completes.
* Identify the persistence mechanism separately; self-deletion implies the payload survives some other way, and that mechanism is the actual target for remediation.
* Where only the deletion artefact remains (a stub batch script, a scheduled-task residue), treat it as a pivot to find what it deleted and when.
data.short_recommendation: Capture the binary before the deletion trigger fires, and find the separate persistence mechanism that survives it.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Spawned a short-lived batch script to delete its own executable after the primary payload had launched from a separate persistence location.

mbc_techniques.implementation: Deleted its own file on disk via a spawned helper process once persistence had been established elsewhere.
